paragraphs: Alyosha led Father Zossima to his bedroom and settled him on the bed. The room was small and held only the bare necessities: a narrow iron bedstead with a strip of felt for a mattress, and in the corner, under the ikons, a reading-desk with a cross and the Gospel lying on it. The elder sank onto the bed, worn out. His eyes shone and his breath came hard. He gazed at Alyosha closely, as if turning something over in his mind.
“Go, dear boy, go. Porfiry is all I need. Be quick, they need you over there. Go and wait on the Father Superior’s table.”
“Let me stay with you,” Alyosha pleaded.

“You are of more use over there. There is no peace in that place. You will wait at table and make yourself useful. If evil spirits rise up, say a prayer. And remember this, my son”—the elder liked to call him that—“you do not belong here in the time to come. When God wills to call me, leave the monastery. Leave it for good.”
Alyosha gave a start.

“Why do you look so? This is not your place for now. I bless you for great service out in the world. Yours will be a long pilgrimage. You will have to take a wife as well. You must bear _all_ of it before you return. There will be much to do. But I have no doubt of you, and that is why I send you forth. Christ is with you. Do not abandon Him, and He will not abandon you. You will see great sorrow, and in that sorrow you will be happy. This is my last word to you: seek happiness in sorrow. Work, and work without rest. Remember my words. I will speak with you again, but not only my days, even my hours, are numbered.”
Again strong emotion showed in Alyosha’s face. His lips quivered at the corners.

“What is it this time?” Father Zossima asked with a gentle smile. “Worldly people may follow their dead weeping, but here we rejoice for a father who is leaving us. We rejoice and we pray for him. Now leave me, for I must pray. Go, and be quick. Stay near your brothers—and not near one of them only, but near both.”

Father Zossima lifted his hand to bless him. Alyosha could raise no objection, though he badly wanted to stay. He also wanted to ask what the elder’s bow to Dmitri meant. The question was on the tip of his tongue, yet he did not dare. He knew the elder would have explained it without being asked, had he thought it right. Evidently it was not his will. That act had left a terrible impression on Alyosha, who believed blindly that it had a mysterious meaning. Mysterious, and perhaps dreadful.

As he hurried out of the hermitage grounds, to reach the monastery in time to serve at the Father Superior’s dinner, a sudden pang struck his heart and he stopped short. He seemed to hear Father Zossima’s words once more, foretelling his end. What the elder had foretold so exactly was bound to happen. Alyosha believed that without any doubt. But how was he to be left without him? How could he live without seeing and hearing him? Where was he to go? The elder had told him not to weep, and to leave the monastery. Good God! He had not known such anguish for a long time. He hurried through the copse between the hermitage and the monastery. He could not bear the burden of his thoughts, and he fixed his eyes on the old pines beside the path. He had not far to go, about five hundred paces. He expected to meet nobody at that hour, but at the first bend in the path he saw Rakitin, who was waiting for someone.
“Are you waiting for me?” Alyosha asked as he caught up.

“Yes,” Rakitin said with a grin. “You’re hurrying to the Father Superior’s, I know; he’s laid on a banquet. There hasn’t been one like it since he entertained the Bishop and General Pahatov. Remember? I won’t be there, but you go and pass the sauces. Tell me one thing, Alexey. What does that vision mean? That’s what I want to ask.”
“What vision?”
“That bowing to your brother Dmitri. And didn’t he tap the ground with his forehead, too!”
“You’re speaking of Father Zossima?”
“Yes, Father Zossima.”
“Tapped the ground?”
“Ah, that’s disrespectful, is it? So what? Anyway, what does the vision mean?”
“I don’t know what it means, Misha.”

“I knew he wouldn’t explain it to you! Of course there’s nothing marvelous in it, only the usual holy mummery. But the show had a point. Every pious soul in town will talk about it and spread the tale around the province, asking what it meant. In my opinion the old man does have a keen nose. He smelled a crime. Your house reeks of it.”
“What crime?”
Rakitin clearly had something he was dying to say.

“It’ll come in your family, this crime. Between your brothers and your rich old father. That’s why Father Zossima flopped down, to be ready for whatever turns up. If something does happen later, they’ll say: ‘Ah, the holy man saw it coming, he prophesied it!’ A poor sort of prophecy, though, just flopping down. ‘Ah, but it was symbolic,’ they’ll say, ‘an allegory,’ and the devil knows what else! They’ll remember it to his glory: ‘He foretold the crime and marked out the criminal!’ It’s always the way with these crazy fanatics. They cross themselves at the tavern and throw stones at the temple. Your elder’s the same: he takes a stick to a just man and falls at the feet of a murderer.”
“What crime? What murderer? What are you saying?”
Alyosha halted. Rakitin halted, too.

“What murderer? As if you didn’t know! I’d bet you’ve thought of it already. That’s interesting, by the way. Listen, Alyosha. You always speak the truth, though you always sit between two stools. Have you thought of it or not? Answer me.”
“I have,” Alyosha answered quietly. Even Rakitin was startled.
“What? You really have?” he cried.
“I ... I haven’t quite thought it,” Alyosha mumbled, “but as soon as you began to talk so oddly, it seemed to me I had thought of it myself.”
“There, you see? (And how neatly you said it!) You looked at your father and your brother Mitya today and thought of a crime. So I’m right?”
“But wait, wait a moment,” Alyosha cut in uneasily. “What makes you see all this? Why does it matter to you? That’s my first question.”

“Two questions, separate but natural enough. I’ll answer one at a time. What made me see it? I’d never have seen it if I hadn’t suddenly understood your brother Dmitri, looked straight into the heart of him in a flash. I got the whole man from one trait. These very honest but passionate people have a line they must not cross. If he crossed it, he’d run at your father with a knife. And your father’s a drunken, shameless old sinner who has never been able to hold back at any line. If both of them let go, they’ll both end badly.”
“No, Misha, no. If that’s all, you’ve set my mind at rest. It won’t come to that.”

“Then why are you shaking? Listen. Our Mitya may be honest (stupid, but honest), but he’s a sensualist. That’s the definition of him, the very core. It’s your father who passed his low sensuality on to him. Do you know, Alyosha, I honestly marvel at how you’ve kept yourself pure. You’re a Karamazov, too, remember! In your family sensuality is a disease. And now these three sensualists are watching each other with knives in their belts. The three of them have their heads knocking together, and you may be the fourth.”
“You’re mistaken about that woman. Dmitri—despises her,” Alyosha said, with something like a shudder.

“Grushenka? No, brother, he doesn’t despise her. He openly threw over his betrothed for her; he can’t despise her. There’s something here you don’t yet understand, my dear boy. A man falls in love with a beauty, with a woman’s body, or even just a part of a woman’s body (a sensualist will understand that), and for her he’ll give up his own children, sell his father and mother, and his country, Russia, too. If he’s honest, he’ll steal for her; if he’s humane, he’ll murder; if he’s faithful, he’ll deceive. Pushkin, the poet of women’s feet, sang of their feet in his verse. Others don’t sing about them, yet they can’t look at a woman’s feet without a thrill—and it’s not only the feet. Contempt doesn’t help here, brother, even if he did despise Grushenka. He does, but he can’t tear himself away.”
“I understand that,” Alyosha suddenly blurted.

“Do you really? Well, I suppose you do, since you blurt it out at the very first word,” said Rakitin with spite. “It slipped out of you without your noticing, and that makes the confession all the more precious. So it’s a familiar subject, you’ve already thought about it, about sensuality, I mean! Oh, you virgin soul! You’re the quiet type, Alyosha, a saint, I know, but the devil alone knows what you’ve thought about and what you already know! You’re pure, but you’ve been down into the depths.... I’ve been watching you for a long time. You’re a Karamazov yourself, a thorough Karamazov. No doubt birth and selection have something to answer for. From your father you get the sensualist, from your mother the crazy saint. Why are you shaking? Is it true, then? And do you know, Grushenka has been begging me to bring you along. ‘I’ll pull off his cassock,’ she says. You can’t think how she keeps begging me to bring you. I wondered why she was so interested in you. Do you know, she’s an extraordinary woman, too!”
“Thank her, and tell her I’m not coming,” Alyosha said with a forced smile. “Finish what you were saying, Misha. I’ll tell you my own idea afterward.”

“There’s nothing to finish. It’s all clear; it’s the same old tune, brother. If even you are a sensualist at heart, what about your brother Ivan? He’s a Karamazov, too. The root of the whole lot of you Karamazovs is that you’re sensual, grasping and crazy! Your brother Ivan writes theological articles for a joke, with some idiotic private motive of his own, though he’s an atheist and admits himself that it’s a fraud. That’s your brother Ivan. He’s trying to win Mitya’s betrothed for himself, and I think he’ll manage it. And what’s more, he’ll have Mitya’s consent. Mitya will hand his betrothed over to be rid of her, and run off to Grushenka. He’s ready to do that in spite of all his nobility and unselfishness. Mark that. Those are the deadliest people! Who the devil can figure you out? He sees his own vileness and carries on with it! And I’ll tell you something else: the old man, your father, is standing in Mitya’s way now. He has suddenly gone mad over Grushenka. His mouth waters when he sees her. It’s purely on her account that he made that scene in the cell just now, because Miüsov called her an ‘abandoned creature.’ He’s worse than a tom-cat in love. At first she only worked for him, on his taverns and some other shady business. Now he has suddenly realized what she is, and he’s wild about her. He keeps pestering her with offers, not honorable ones, naturally. And on that road they’ll crash into each other, the precious father and son! But Grushenka favors neither. She’s still playing with them, teasing them both and calculating which will get her more. She could filch a lot of money from the papa, but he wouldn’t marry her, and in the end he may turn stingy and keep his purse shut. That’s where Mitya’s worth comes in. He has no money, but he’s ready to marry her. Yes, ready to marry her! To drop his betrothed, a rare beauty, Katerina Ivanovna, rich and a colonel’s daughter, and marry Grushenka, who has been the mistress of that dissolute old merchant Samsonov, a coarse, uneducated provincial mayor. A murderous clash may very well come out of all this, and that’s exactly what your brother Ivan is waiting for. It would suit him down to the ground. He’ll carry off Katerina Ivanovna, whom he’s pining for, and pocket her dowry of sixty thousand. That’s a great temptation to begin with, for a man of no account and a beggar. And note this: he won’t be wronging Mitya, he’ll be doing him the greatest favor. I know for a fact that only last week Mitya got drunk in a tavern with some gypsy girls and shouted out that he was unworthy of his betrothed, Katya, but that his brother Ivan was the man who deserved her. And Katerina Ivanovna won’t refuse in the end a man as fascinating as Ivan. She’s wavering between the two already. And how has that Ivan won all of you, so that you all worship him? He’s laughing at you, enjoying himself at your expense.”
